## A credential per machine, and a node per window

**This release changes how zyris-code pairs with Attacca, and a build older than 0.4.0
enrols again.** A credential file left by a version from before credentials existed is
not read, so on first launch the enrollment panel appears once: pick (or create) the
system this machine is in, approve every scope, and that issues one `zc_` credential
for the program `zyris-code` on that system. The browser is not needed again unless
the credential is revoked.

**Every window is a node of its own**, named after the directory it was started in and
shown in Attacca as `<system>/zyris-code/<directory>` — `laptop/zyris-code/myrepo`. A
second window in the same directory becomes `myrepo-2` for as long as both are open;
`ZYRIS_NODE_NAME` overrides the last part. Nothing stands by any more.

Two windows used to share one credential, and therefore one node, and the one that
arrived second took the routing — the earlier window kept drawing, kept its history,
and received no tool calls. Each window registers its own node now. The agent sees
every node's tools under one name and picks the computer with each tool's `node_path`,
and the session preamble and the `rules` tool say which path is the one you are sitting
at. `ZYRIS_NODE_TOKEN` is gone: a `zc_` credential issued in Attacca goes in
`ZYRIS_CREDENTIAL`, or in a file named by `ZYRIS_CREDENTIAL_FILE`, instead of enrolling.

## It stops assuming a fast terminal

A local terminal is drawn at 60fps and one over SSH at 20, with streamed content
batched under either — on a slow link it is the link that breaks, not the drawing. Each
frame is bracketed in DEC's synchronized update (`CSI ?2026h/l`), so a repaint lands as
one picture rather than cells arriving one after another, which is what `claude` and
`codex` do in the same terminal. The residue a wide glyph leaves when it shrinks is
healed a few cells at a time where it happens, instead of overwriting the whole screen
whenever anything was drawn — that sweep is what read as flicker. A selection survives
the frames now, so the usage poll and streaming deltas no longer end a drag before it
can be copied, and the press that gave the window focus cannot fold a card nobody aimed
at.

## The MCP and plugin panels are managers, not lists to read

Both panels carry a cursor and keys that act on the row under it, where everything used
to be a command with a name typed after it — `/mcp on <name>`, `/plugin remove <name>` —
or editing a JSON file by hand. The MCP panel shows one row per server, says where it
came from, the whole invocation and the names of what it is handed (names, never
values), and `Enter` switches it while `d` takes it out of the file it is written in.
The plugin panel shows a row per plugin with its manifest's version, author, repository
and licence, `Enter` switches it on or off, `u` pulls a fetched plugin's update and `d`
deletes its directory after asking. A fetched plugin can now be switched **off** without
deleting it; until this release the only way to stop one contributing was to remove its
directory.

## What you press

- **`Esc` is the only key that stops a turn.** `Ctrl+C` no longer cancels: its first
  press arms quitting and the second quits, so the one that cannot be taken back is not
  the one pressed by mistake. A card cut with `Esc` reads `Stopped`, not `Done`.
- **A double click takes the row under the pointer**, and the drag wash is no longer the
  same colour as the band a message you sent is drawn in.
- `ZYRIS_CODE_TRACE=term,keys,mouse` writes what the terminal actually sent — the
  environment it was read as, every key event, and for the mouse both the event and the
  cell the hit-test made of it. It goes to stderr and `$TMPDIR/zyris-code-trace.log`,
  never onto the screen.
- A job belongs to the conversation that asked for it, so the activity line stops
  narrating another thread's build as this one's work; `report_result` is a row of the
  conversation rather than a card over the input.
- The `edit` tool answers a failed match with the nearest text and forgives whitespace,
  a capability is read out of a versioned tool name again, and no tool declares a call
  limit — every tool answers in English.
